# Decoding Toyota Corolla 2006 Fuse Box Abbreviations

Working on an older vehicle often feels like reverse-engineering a legacy system where documentation is sparse or relies heavily on industry shorthand. If you are attempting to replace a fuse in a 2006 Toyota Corolla, the diagram inside the under-dash fuse box will likely look like a cryptic list of codes rather than clear labels. Understanding these abbreviations isn't just about reading; it's about mapping electrical loads to their specific vehicle subsystems to ensure you don't cut power to something critical while trying to fix a minor issue.

The most common confusion arises from the two-column layout found in many Toyota fuse boxes of this era, labeled **AM1** and **AM2**. These do not stand for "Amperage 1" or "Amperage 2." Instead, they refer to **Accessory Mode 1** and **Accessory Mode 2**, which correspond to different ignition switch positions.

When the key is in the "ACC" (Accessory) position, only circuits under AM1 are active. This typically powers aftermarket audio systems, memory windows, or interior lighting that should remain functional without starting the engine. Moving the key to the "ON" position activates both AM1 and AM2, bringing the rest of the vehicle's accessories online. If you pull a fuse from an AM2 slot while the car is in ACC mode, nothing will happen until you turn the ignition further. This distinction is crucial when diagnosing why a specific accessory fails; checking the switch position relative to the fuse column is step one before inspecting the component itself.

Several codes on your list relate directly to power distribution and control modules:

*   **P/W** stands for Power Window. In modern vehicles, this often includes the master switch circuit as well as individual motor drivers. If this fuse blows frequently, check for a short in the window regulator motors or a stuck relay before replacing the fuse again.
*   **ECU-IG** and **ECU-B** are dedicated to the Engine Control Unit (ECU). "IG" indicates Ignition power supplied when the key is turned on, while "B" stands for Battery constant power, which remains active even with the car off (for memory retention of radio presets or ECU adaptation values). Never replace these fuses unless you have verified there is a hard short to ground; doing so repeatedly can trigger immobilizer codes.
*   **INV** refers to the Inverter. In a 2006 Corolla, this usually powers the air conditioning compressor clutch or the variable valve timing (VVT) solenoids, depending on the specific engine code (1ZZ-FE vs. 2ZR-FE). A blown INV fuse will result in an AC that blows hot air or an engine running rough at idle due to lost VVT control.
*   **P/POINT** is the ignition coil driver circuit. If this fails, you won't get a spark. This is a high-current load, so verify your multimeter settings can handle the peak current if testing continuity on live circuits.

Other abbreviations serve specific subsystems:

*   **CIG** powers the cigarette lighter and ashtray socket.
*   **GAUGE** drives the instrument cluster illumination and sensors. If this blows, your warning lights or speedometer may go dark, but usually not the needles themselves unless they share a ground.
*   **OBD** provides power to the On-Board Diagnostics port. This is vital for any diagnostic tool connection.

When replacing these fuses, always use the exact amperage rating printed on the fuse box cover diagram. Substituting a higher amp fuse might protect the wiring harness from blowing but will destroy the downstream electrical component (like a headlight bulb or sensor) once it draws too much current. Conversely, using a lower amp fuse will cause nuisance tripping and leave you stranded.

If your vehicle has a hybrid variant or specific regional trim levels not standard in North America, additional fuses may appear for high-voltage components, though the 2006 model year generally lacks these in the under-dash box unless it is a specific international market export. Always cross-reference the physical fuse location with the diagram on the inside of the cover to avoid pulling the wrong module power source. For further assistance interpreting complex wiring diagrams for legacy vehicles, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide structured data access tools that help visualize these electrical trees more clearly than a static paper manual.
